title: United Express 6291
summary: United Express Flight 6291, a BAe Jetstream 41, crashed while approaching Columbus in poor weather. During descent through 1,250 feet, the stick shaker activated twice, indicating an aerodynamic stall. The crew, inexperienced with electronic flight instruments, misdiagnosed the stall warning and failed to apply proper recovery procedures. The aircraft descended in a high nose-up attitude and struck trees 1.2 miles short of the runway.
probable_cause: The crew's failure to properly recognize and respond to the stall warning, the pilot-in-command's failure to exercise proper command authority and judgment, inadequate training and standardization in the airline's pilot training program, and the crew's continued attempts at an unstable approach without executing a timely go-around. (p. 50-51)

factors.evidence: The crew conducted a poorly planned and unstable approach to runway 28L with reduced visibility and ceiling of 800 feet and 2.5 miles visibility. (p. 20)
The crew failed to maintain both proper airspeed and altitude during descent, not following standard instrument scan procedures. (p. 21)
The aircraft continued to descend below the prescribed glide slope in a high nose-up attitude, indicating a decaying energy state. (p. 21)
Stick shaker activated and sounded for 3 seconds at 1,250 feet descending. After 1.5 seconds of silence, it sounded again, indicating the aircraft was in a stall condition. (p. 22)
Almost immediately after stall warning activated, Captain White asked in an alarmed manner, 'Tony! What did you do?' indicating misdiagnosis of the stall condition. (p. 22)

Neither pilot performed proper stall recovery procedure; instead, they continued forward control inputs and descent. The captain's recovery attempt was ineffective and improper, pulling back on yoke too late. (p. 23)
Both pilots lacked experience with electronic flight instrument systems; the Jetstream 41 first officer had recently joined the airline, and captain had history of failed check rides. (p. 18-19)
Aircraft collided with stand of trees in a high nose-up attitude at approximately 900 feet AGL, 1.2 miles short of runway 28L threshold. (p. 25)

events.text: Flight 6291 departed from Dulles at 9:58 p.m. EST on scheduled 90-minute flight to Columbus
Columbus Approach Control contacted; captain advised descending through 13,200 feet. Controller assigned 285-degree heading to intercept ILS runway 28L and cleared to 10,000 feet
Updated weather reported cloud overcast 800 feet, visibility 2.5 miles in light snow and fog, wind 300 degrees at 4 knots
Runway 28L ILS approach clearance issued; clearance to land granted two minutes later
Aircraft descending through 1,250 feet, stick shaker activated and sounded for 3 seconds
Captain asked in alarmed manner, 'Tony! What did you do?', indicating misdiagnosis of stall warning
After 1.5 seconds of silence, stick shaker sounded again, confirming persistent stall condition
Aircraft collided with stand of trees in high nose-up attitude, 1.2 miles short of runway 28L; 5 of 8 occupants killed

recommendations.text: Airlines should develop and implement pilot training programs that specifically address recognition and recovery from aerodynamic stalls at low altitudes.
The FAA should review and revise minimum training requirements for pilots operating multi-engine aircraft to ensure adequate stall awareness and recovery training.
Airlines should develop standardized approach procedures that include minimum criteria for approach stability and mandatory go-around procedures when these criteria are not met.
Cockpit resource management training should emphasize proper command authority, crew coordination, and decision-making during emergency situations.

safety_changes: Enhanced pilot training requirements for stall recognition and recovery
Development of approach stability standards across the industry
